hints: Count four consecutive elements in Period 4 that fit an $M_2O_3$ amphoteric oxide and an $MO_2$ acidic oxide, starting from the soft low melting metal.
walkthrough:
Use the clues for D**
Think of a soft silvery metal in Period 4 that melts just above room temperature (about $30^{\circ}\text{C}$) and forms a $+3$ oxide $\text{D}_2\text{O}_3$. That is gallium, $\text{Ga}$, which sits just after the transition metals. Its oxide is amphoteric, just like $\text{Al}_2\text{O}_3$ above it in Group 13.

Use the clues for G and check the sequence**
A solid with $\text{G}_8$ molecules that burns to an acidic dioxide $\text{GO}_2$ points to a Group 16 element like sulfur. In Period 4 that is selenium, $\text{Se}$. Check the run: $\text{Ga}$ (D), $\text{Ge}$ (E), $\text{As}$ (F), $\text{Se}$ (G) gives four consecutive Period 4 elements, which fits perfectly.
Final answer: D is $\text{Ga}$ and G is $\text{Se}$.

hints: When an amphoteric oxide meets an acid it behaves as a base, so predict a salt plus water in the same way as $\text{Al}_2\text{O}_3$ with $\text{HCl}$.
Write the formulae $\text{D}_2\text{O}_3$, $\text{HCl}$, $\text{DCl}_3$ and $\text{H}_2\text{O}$ first, then balance D, then H and Cl together.
walkthrough:
See the oxide acting as a base**
Here $\text{D}_2\text{O}_3$ meets an acid, so it shows its basic side. A basic metal oxide plus acid always gives salt plus water. So you get gallium chloride plus water: $\text{D}_2\text{O}_3 + \text{HCl} \rightarrow \text{DCl}_3 + \text{H}_2\text{O}$ as the skeleton.

Balance carefully**
There are $2$ D on the left, so you need $2\text{DCl}_3$ on the right. That needs $6$ Cl, so use $6\text{HCl}$ on the left. That gives $6$ H, which makes $3\text{H}_2\text{O}$. The finished equation is $$\text{D}_2\text{O}_3 + 6\text{HCl} \rightarrow 2\text{DCl}_3 + 3\text{H}_2\text{O}$$

hints: When the same oxide meets concentrated alkali it behaves as an acid, so expect a gallate type salt plus water, analogous to aluminate formation.
Use the simplest gallate form $\text{NaDO}_2$ as product and balance Na, D, O and H starting from $\text{D}_2\text{O}_3 + \text{NaOH}$.
walkthrough:
See the oxide acting as an acid**
Now the same $\text{D}_2\text{O}_3$ meets $\text{NaOH}$, so it shows its acidic side. Just as $\text{Al}_2\text{O}_3$ gives $\text{NaAlO}_2$, here you get sodium gallate. The simplest accepted form is $\text{NaDO}_2$ plus water.

Balance the skeleton**
Start with $$\text{D}_2\text{O}_3 + \text{NaOH} \rightarrow \text{NaDO}_2 + \text{H}_2\text{O}$$ You need $2$ D on the right, so put $2$ in front of $\text{NaDO}_2$. That needs $2$ Na, so use $2\text{NaOH}$. Oxygen and hydrogen then balance with $1\text{H}_2\text{O}$: $$\text{D}_2\text{O}_3 + 2\text{NaOH} \rightarrow 2\text{NaDO}_2 + \text{H}_2\text{O}$$

hints: Compare the very high melting point of $1900^{\circ}\text{C}$ with typical simple molecular oxides to decide between strong lattice forces and weak intermolecular forces.
walkthrough:
Let the melting point tell the story**
A melting point of $1900^{\circ}\text{C}$ is huge. If $\text{D}_2\text{O}_3$ were simple molecules, only weak van der Waals forces would hold the molecules together and it would melt very easily. To stay solid to $1900^{\circ}\text{C}$ it must have a giant lattice of oppositely charged ions, $\text{D}^{3+}$ and $\text{O}^{2-}$, held by very strong ionic bonds in all directions.
Final answer: Giant ionic lattice (ionic with strong ionic bonding).

hints: Recall that a non-metal dioxide that gives a $\text{Na}_2\text{GO}_3$ salt with alkali must first form the acid $\text{H}_2\text{GO}_3$ with water.
walkthrough:
Form the acid by adding water**
$\text{GO}_2$ is an acidic oxide, like $\text{SO}_2$ or $\text{CO}_2$. It reacts with water by simple addition to give the corresponding oxoacid. Since the sodium salt is $\text{Na}_2\text{GO}_3$, the parent acid must be $\text{H}_2\text{GO}_3$: $$\text{GO}_2 + \text{H}_2\text{O} \rightarrow \text{H}_2\text{GO}_3$$ In real symbols this is $\text{SeO}_2 + \text{H}_2\text{O} \rightarrow \text{H}_2\text{SeO}_3$.
